section: An Information Transmission View on Orthogonal Finetuning
section_text:
We start with some preliminaries of OFT. To finetune the pretrained weight matrix, OFT reparameterizes the new weight matrix as the product of a learnable orthogonal matrix and the frozen pretrained weight matrix. Compared to LoRA which updates the weights with an additive low-rank matrix, OFT uses a multiplicative orthogonal matrix to update the weights. To achieve parameter-efficiency, LoRA uses a low-rank structure, and in contrast, the original OFT uses a block-diagonal orthogonal structure~\cite{qiu2023controlling} (the smaller the size of diagonal blocks is, the more parameter-efficient OFT is). An intuitive comparison is given in Figure~\ref{fig:comp_lora}. The motivation for applying orthogonal transformation to finetune the weight matrix is to preserve the pair-wise angles of neurons~\cite{liu2018learning,liu2021orthogonal,qiu2023controlling}, such that the semantic knowledge from pretraining can be largely preserved. Concretely, OFT optimizes an orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ for a pretrained linear layer $\bm{W}^0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$, and modifies the forward pass from $\bm{z}=(\bm{W}^0)^\top\bm{x}$ to $\bm{z}=(\bm{R}\bm{W}^0)^\top\bm{x}$, where $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are the input and output vector, respectively. To achieve zero initialization, OFT initializes $\bm{R}$ as an identity matrix. To ensure the orthogonality of $\bm{R}$ throughout the finetuning process, we follow \cite{qiu2023controlling,liu2021orthogonal} to employ Cayley parameterization, \emph{i.e.}, $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$ where $\bm{Q}$ is a skew-symmetric matrix with $\bm{Q}=-\bm{Q}^\top$. For parameter-efficiency, the block-diagonal structure is introduced by parameterizing the orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$ as $\text{diag}(\bm{R}_1,\bm{R}_2,\cdots,\bm{R}_r)$ where $\bm{R}_i\in\mathcal{R}^{b\times b},\forall i$ is a small orthogonal matrix and $br=d$. The parameter-efficiency brought by the block-diagonal structure comes at a price -- it introduces an assumption that the dimensions of a neuron (\emph{i.e.}, a column vector of the weight matrix $\bm{W}^0$) are divided by $r$ groups and dimensions in different groups are transformed separately using different orthogonal matrices. Despite the empirical effectiveness of the block-diagonal structure, it makes no sense to divide the dimensions of a neuron into $r$ groups based on their indices, which makes dense orthogonal matrices desirable. A natural question arises: \emph{Can we construct a dense orthogonal matrix without losing the parameter-efficiency?}

To address this question, we propose to compose a dense orthogonal matrix with a product of multiple sparse orthogonal matrices. To provide a unified yet intuitive perspective to study the sparsity pattern of orthogonal matrix factorization, we frame the problem of generating a dense orthogonal matrix in OFT as an information transmission problem. Specifically, generating a dense matrix $\bm{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ by a product of $m$ square matrices $\thickmuskip=2mu \medmuskip=2mu \bm{R}=\bm{B}_m\bm{B}_{m-1}\cdots\bm{B}_1$ can be viewed as transmitting information in a grid with $d\times (m+1)$ nodes, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans}. The motivation behind the information transmission view comes from the observation that a $d$-dimensional dense square matrix can be interpreted as a dense connectivity from $d$ nodes to another $d$ nodes. For the matrix $\bm{R}$, if the element $R_{ij}$ is zero, then it indicates that information from the $j$-th node cannot flow to the $i$-th node. If $R_{ij}$ is non-zero, then the information can be transmitted. Therefore, representing the dense matrix $\bm{R}$ with multiple matrices $\bm{B}_m\bm{B}_{m-1}\cdots\bm{B}_1$ can also be interpreted as performing sequential information exchange based on the graphs induced by $\bm{B}_i, \forall i$. The information flows following $\bm{B}_1$ first and $\bm{B}_n$ in the end. As a concrete example in Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans}, we consider the factorization $\bm{R}=\bm{B}_5\bm{B}_4\bm{B}_3\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$ whose sparsity patterns and induced graph are visualized. The graph in Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans} is the result of unrolling the matrix multiplication. In the induced graph, the matrix $\bm{B}_i$ is viewed as the connectivity matrix from the $i$-th level nodes to the $(i+1)$-th level nodes. More specifically, the $(j_1,j_2)$ element of $\bm{B}_i$ denotes whether there is a directed edge from the $j_2$-th node in the $i$-th level to the $j_1$-th node in the $(i+1)$-th level (zero means no edge). For $\bm{B}_5\bm{B}_4\bm{B}_3\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$ to be a dense matrix, every node in the first level should be able to transmit information to all the nodes in the $6$-th level. If we only consider $\bm{R}=\bm{B}_4\bm{B}_3\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$ which corresponds to the source nodes in the first level and the receiver nodes in $5$-th level, then we find that information from the node $1$ cannot be transmitted to the node $3$. Therefore, the sparsity pattern of $\bm{B}_4\bm{B}_3\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$ has a zero element at the $(3,1)$ position. Considering $\bm{R}=\bm{B}_3\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$ and $\bm{R}=\bm{B}_2\bm{B}_1$, the same correspondence holds between the induced graph and the sparsity pattern. Generally, for a matrix $\bm{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ to be dense, the $m$ factorization matrices $\bm{B}_m,\cdots,\bm{B}_1$ needs to correspond to a set of directed edges on a $d\times (m+1)$ grid where one directed edge can only connect two nodes between adjacent levels (\emph{i.e.}, columns), such that information from every node in the first level can be transmitted to every node in the $(m+1)$-th level.

The information transmission view can help us gain a better understanding of the sparsity pattern of factorization matrices in OFT. Figure~\ref{fig:blk_diag} visualizes the block-diagonal structure of $\bm{R}$ in the original OFT. Despite reducing the number of trainable parameters, the block-diagonal structure cannot construct a dense matrix $\bm{R}$. Our goal is to compose a dense orthogonal matrix with $m$ sparse orthogonal matrices, using as few effective trainable parameters as possible. Under the information transmission view, the general desiderata towards our goal are \emph{(i)} \textbf{dense connectivity}: every node in the first level has at least one path to every node in the last level, and \emph{(ii)} \textbf{minimum free edges}: the total number of edges should be as small as possible under the orthogonality constraint. We note that orthogonality injects a delicate constraint to the edges between adjacent levels. For example, for each matrix $\bm{B}_i$ to be full-rank (a necessary condition of orthogonality), we need to have $d$ edges to form a bijection between all the nodes in the $i$-th level and all the nodes in the $(i=1)$-th level, which makes the number of edges between adjacent levels at least $d$ (\emph{e.g.}, 4 for the example in Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans}). These $d$ edges is necessary for orthogonality and should not be counted into the number of edges, because these elements are not trainable (\emph{e.g.}, for a $d\times d$ orthogonal with $d$ non-zero entries, these entries can only be $\pm 1$). Because orthogonal matrices require less number of parameters than full matrices, the orthogonality constraint will bring in additional dependency among edges. As an example, for a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix, one zero at the $(1,1)$ position will imply another zero at the $(2,2)$ position (\emph{i.e.}, one missing edge could imply another missing edge). Therefore, for each feasible set of edge connections, the orthogonality may sometimes add or remove some edges. By visualizing the non-zero pattern of the composed orthogonal matrix, the information transmission framework is particularly useful in OFT, because we only care about the non-zero trainable elements of $\bm{R}$ and their specific values do not matter.

A naive dense connection between two levels takes $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ edges (\emph{i.e.}, a single dense orthogonal matrix), yielding $d^2-d$ edges (for $d=4$, it is 12 edges). Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans} gives an example of a feasible matrix factorization and it takes $10$ edges in total, which is actually less than a single dense orthogonal matrix. This framework enables us to study the parameter-efficiency of OFT from a graphical perspective, and we can easily come up with feasible factorizations with this framework. We draw inspiration from an interesting topology from the Cooley-Tukey algorithm, called butterfly graphs~\cite{cooley1965algorithm}, which can densely connect $d$ source nodes and $d$ receiver nodes efficiently with $\mathcal{O}(d\log d)$ edges. For example, the topology in Figure~\ref{fig:info_trans} takes $10$ edges to achieve dense connectivity, while the butterfly network only takes $8$ edges. Next, we introduce how the butterfly structure can improve parameter efficiency.
